extracted.intended_audience: aspiring writers, literary critics, and educated readers interested in the moral/esthetic qualities of literary heroes
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts prescriptive criteria for what makes a literary 'Hero' and how Men of Letters should live and write: authenticity, moral courage, practical prudence, and the relation of faith and doubt. Useful as guidance for creative writers and critics assessing greatness in authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity / heart-sincerity
rubrics_metrics.description: The sincere man speaks from the heart of Nature; he is open to Nature and incapable of being insincere—'heart-sincerity' is primary material for great men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle repeatedly treats sincerity as essential: Johnson and Mahomet share 'heart-sincerity' despite doctrinal differences. Anti-patterns: hearsay, mere plausibility, 'half-truths' and simulations. Scoring note: value genuine feeling and unforced truthfulness in voice and conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief as enabling action (vs. perpetual scepticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief is 'the healthy act of a man's mind' enabling genuine action; excessive scepticism produces 'spiritual paralysis' that prevents heroic activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doubt is part of arriving at belief, but public parading of doubt (endless debate) is harmful. Writers should cultivate convictions sufficient to act (write/speak) rather than remain forever in argumentative skep­sis. Examples: the Eighteenth Century's scepticism produced quackery and paralysis; remedy is regaining a believing, sincere outlook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality as genuineness, not mere novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Originality is not simply being 'new' but being 'genuine'—grounded in truth and nature rather than novelty for its own sake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle: 'The essence of originality is not that it be new.' Johnson believed in old truths but was original through sincerity. Anti-pattern: novelty without substance. Scoring: prefer works that feel authentically rooted even when traditional in form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength = calm endurance and capacity, not mere vehemence
rubrics_metrics.description: True strength in a writer or hero is calm, sustained capacity to bear difficulty ('he that can walk under the heaviest weight without staggering'), not spasmodic intensity or convulsive vehemence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast Rousseau (intense, spasmodic) with the ideal of steady force. Talent of silence and restraint is part of strength. Penalize uncontrolled outbursts, reward measured force and persistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral prudence: do what can be done; clear your mind of cant
rubrics_metrics.description: In an age where little is known, the Gospel to preach is practical moral prudence: act; 'in a world where much is to be done, and little is to be known,' learn how to do it and avoid cant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnson's teaching: prioritize concrete action over empty rhetoric. Creative practitioners should favor practicable moral purpose and honest workmanship over grandiose but hollow declarations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulas and style must contain substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulas (styles, received forms) begin full of substance; they are legitimate when they articulate a real inner fact — they become idolatrous only when emptied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable: Johnson's 'buckram style' may be grandiloquent but has 'something within it.' Anti-pattern: elegant style with no content. When evaluating, test whether form serves an inner truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophetic function of the writer (voice of truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Men of Letters can function as Prophets—speakers of 'everlasting truth'—whose authentic utterances plant a seed for future generations; the writer's role can be sociopolitical guidance as well as aesthetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle calls Johnson, Rousseau and Burns 'Prophets' of their age. Guidance: reward writing that bears moral or civil insight and has the gravitas to influence society; anti-pattern is purely self-regarding or ephemeral writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poverty and struggle as an ordeal/creative crucible
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic hardship and the 'ordeal' of literary life can be a necessary trial that forges strong men; struggle from lower classes often produces talent that should be recognized and allowed to prove itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle argues society should not remove all struggle (money can't do everything); instead recognize and test talent. For creators: adversity is not necessarily disqualifying and may produce depth; for institutions: provide means to discover and support deserving talent (avoid the worst regulation which leaves it to blind chance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of quackery, simulacrum and mimicry
rubrics_metrics.description: The age of scepticism breeds 'quacks' and simulacra—performative, mimetic acting that substitutes for genuine action; avoid such mimicry in thought and style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cagliostro, political theatricality such as Chatham's. In writing, penalize mere sentimentality, theatrical posturing, and imitation that lacks inner conviction; reward authenticity and substance-driven expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talent of silence / restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: A valuable quality is the ability to 'hold his peace' until the proper moment; restraint prevents premature or destructive expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle criticizes Rousseau for lacking this. In creative work, judge favorably those who show disciplined restraint and timing in revelation and rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-egoism / humility
rubrics_metrics.description: Egoism (vanity, hunger for praise) is the root of faults and miseries; true greatness requires overcoming desire for praise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rousseau's 'Egoism' is cited as his chief fault. Evaluate writers for humility and resistance to vanity; beware self-aggrandizing rhetoric and acts aimed primarily at flattering reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make adverse conditions 'do for you' (self-help and integrity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Great men make their conditions serve their purpose: they live honestly by their own resources, refusing to beg or falsely demean themselves (e.g., Johnson pitching away gifted shoes rather than accept beggary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage narratives and practices that convert poverty and chaos into a working ground; reward integrity and stoic self-reliance rather than humiliating dependency or compromise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Man of intellect as ideal governor / public utility of writers
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay holds that writers and men of intellect are good candidates for public leadership; discovering and trying such men for governance is promising for society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle cites Chinese examinations as an attempt to promote literati into governance. As a social guideline: institutions should identify and elevate intellectual merit; for writers, cultivate public-spirited understanding and administrative sensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware mechanistic/utilitarian worldview (loss of Godhood and heroism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reducing the universe to mechanism and motives (pure Utilitarianism/Benthamism) strips life of nobility; such a view precludes heroic action and degrades all judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle condemns an exclusively mechanistic account of human motives. In creative practice, avoid collapsing moral worth to mere utility; evaluate works for recognition of transcendent, mysterious, or spiritual dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Being 'in earnest' (wholeheartedness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A primary characteristic of a hero is being 'heartily in earnest'—genuine intensity of commitment to an idea or cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if other traits are flawed (Rousseau is earnest though defective), wholehearted conviction is crucial. Reward works that demonstrate sincere, sustained moral/intellectual urgency rather than lukewarm irony or detached cleverness.
